strengths: Novel problem formulation: First work to recover volumetric muscle deformations from multi-view RGB, addressing a genuine gap in digital human modeling between surface-only and physics-based approaches.

Valuable dataset contribution: SKIM provides comprehensive multi-layer data (skin, muscle, bone) with dense marker tracking, individualized muscle meshes, and ground-truth poses across 45 minutes of motion—a meaningful resource for the community.

Well-motivated technical approach: Decoupled blendshape formulation with biomechanical priors (volume preservation, tangential sliding, bending) is sensible for capturing soft-tissue dynamics; residual estimation in canonical space elegantly separates pose-driven and non-rigid deformations.

Thorough experimental evaluation: Comprehensive metrics (MPME, MedPME, P90, DRE, intersection, volume preservation), detailed ablations clearly showing contribution of each component, and insightful findings (e.g., structural tension most critical for volumetry stability).

Clear presentation and sound technical execution: Well-organized writing, informative pipeline visualization, mathematically correct formulations, and reproducible methodology within the constraints of available hardware.
Practical inference capability: Works from pose input alone, enabling scalable downstream applications in sports medicine and entertainment without requiring marker suits at inference time.
weaknesses: Critical scalability limitations: Only 5 subjects with subject-specific models and no cross-subject generalization study—insufficient for practical deployment and raises serious questions about generalization to diverse body types, sizes, and anatomies.

Impractical marker suit dependency: Custom ArUco-marked suit cannot scale to real-world capture; authors acknowledge markerless alternatives as future work but provide no preliminary evidence, creating a major barrier to adoption despite claiming the dataset could enable markerless trackers.

Lack of volumetric ground truth validation: No in-vivo volumetric measurements; evaluation relies on indirect surface marker tracking. The 10.35% deep muscle layer volume error contradicts claims of anatomical plausibility and is rationalized as a 'compromise' rather than investigated—no comparison with FEM or biomechanical simulators.

Limited motion diversity and coverage: ~9 minutes per subject across 5 subjects; figures show primarily arm motions with no demonstration on lower body or full-body complex actions; unclear generalization to unseen motion patterns even within subjects.

Template initialization vulnerability: Depends on external volumetric fitting [30] with no sensitivity analysis; authors acknowledge potential initialization errors but defer joint optimization to future work, leaving a known weakness unaddressed.

Evaluation methodology concerns: Cross-topology comparison with HIT requires error-prone barycentric mapping; LBS is inadequate as dynamic baseline; metrics are surface-centric rather than measuring true internal anatomical accuracy.

Unresolved disentanglement ambiguity: Authors acknowledge muscle/skin separation is 'inherently ambiguous' but provide no analysis of whether different loss weights yield equally plausible but anatomically different solutions, limiting confidence in the decomposition.

Insufficient technical disclosure: U-Net architecture details, hyperparameter selection strategy, training convergence behavior, inference time, and computational cost not reported—impeding reproducibility and understanding of practical feasibility.

Prohibitive reproducibility barriers: Requires exclusive-access hardware (120-camera mocap, 140-camera scanner); adapting to new subjects demands identical infrastructure, making the method inaccessible to most researchers despite data release.

Missing critical analyses: No generalization guidance for new subjects/body types; no comparison with alternative kinematic deformation methods; no analysis of anatomical validity beyond geometric constraints; no evaluation on occluded or partially visible subjects.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First work to recover dynamic muscle deformations from multi-view RGB video, addressing an important gap between surface-only models and complex volumetric simulations

Comprehensive SKIM dataset with high-quality multi-view annotations including 3D anatomical meshes (skin, muscle, bone), synchronized 120-camera captures at 25 Hz, dense marker tracking, and detailed metadata across 5 subjects

Technically sound method combining decoupled blendshape formulation with well-motivated biomechanical priors (smoothness, bending resistance, volume preservation, tangential sliding constraints) that effectively enforce anatomical plausibility
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-4) clearly demonstrating the contribution of each component, with SOMA achieving 13.43 mm MPME compared to 19.11 mm for LBS baseline

Comprehensive evaluation across multiple metrics (tracking error, volume preservation, intersection ratio, dynamic region error) providing multifaceted assessment of anatomical and geometric plausibility
Clear and well-written presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1, 5, 7) and detailed supplementary material covering implementation details, dataset structure, and additional results
Honest discussion of limitations including subject-specificity, marker suit requirements, and decomposition ambiguities, demonstrating appropriate scientific integrity
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Only 5 subjects (3 male, 2 female) is far below standards for a dataset/benchmark paper at ECCV. Most human body model datasets (SMPL, SCAPE) use 100+ subjects, raising serious concerns about generalization and anatomical diversity

No cross-subject generalization evaluation: All validation occurs on the same 5 subjects with no train/test split across subjects or leave-one-subject-out protocol, despite claiming 'generalization on unseen poses'. This is a fundamental evaluation gap

Subject-specific models severely limit practical applicability: The explicit statement that 'method is currently subject-specific' (Section 6) undermines real-world utility for VR, sports, and medical applications. This critical limitation is acknowledged but inadequately addressed

Marker suit requirement restricts real-world deployment: Custom ArUco-embedded suit is necessary, creating significant practical barrier compared to markerless approaches. Appendix shows incomplete marker coverage (55-85% for curls). No ablation examining necessity of marker data

Unclear anatomical ground truth acquisition: The process for obtaining 3D muscle meshes is never clearly explained (manual segmentation? From what imaging?). No inter-annotator agreement metrics provided if manual annotation used, affecting confidence in ground truth quality

Insufficient and potentially unfair baseline comparisons: HIT [27] is concurrent work (2024 arxiv), SMPL is surface-only and unsuitable for muscle modeling, LBS is too simplistic. Missing comparisons to other anatomy modeling methods, physics-based simulations, or volumetric approaches

Acknowledged decomposition ambiguity inadequately addressed: Section 4 states the muscle/skin decomposition is 'inherently ill-posed,' but provides no quantitative analysis of how this ambiguity affects learned representations or anatomical validity of the decomposition

No theoretical analysis of convergence or failure modes: No discussion of when/why the method succeeds or fails, or theoretical guarantees on the learning process. Only 20 training epochs with no convergence analysis or learning curves provided
Hyperparameter choices lack justification: Loss weights (λ_data=50, λ_smooth=100, etc.) appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis or ablation studies on these critical choices
Limited statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing in results tables. Single test set with no cross-validation details. No repeated runs reported

Modest dataset scale for deep learning: Despite 330K frames, the dataset contains only 5 subjects × 45 minutes. This is modest by modern deep learning standards and may insufficiently support generalizable models

Limited motion diversity: Captured motions focus on warm-up and resistance training exercises, missing diverse activities (ADLs, sports, complex full-body dynamics) necessary to assess generalization to new movement types
Volume preservation metrics lack biological validation: 1.37% claimed error is presented without comparing to real biological measurements or validating physiological meaningfulness
No ethical discussion: Missing analysis of privacy concerns with body imaging or potential misuse (deepfakes, unauthorized body modeling of individuals)
